title: Valid Paranthesis Checker
description:
Given a string s containing only three types of characters: '(', ')' and '*', return true if s is valid.

The following rules define a valid string:

	• Any left parenthesis '(' must have a corresponding right parenthesis ')'.

	• Any right parenthesis ')' must have a corresponding left parenthesis '('.

	• Left parenthesis '(' must go before the corresponding right parenthesis ')'.

	• '*' could be treated as a single right parenthesis ')' or a single left parenthesis '(' or an empty string "".

title: N meetings in one room
description:
Given start[i] and finish[i] for N meetings (a meeting occupies [start, finish) — a new meeting may start exactly when another ends), select the maximum number of meetings a single room can host and print their original 1-based indices in increasing order.

Greedy interval scheduling: sort meetings by finishing time and take each meeting whose start is ≥ the last accepted meeting's finish. Earliest-finish-first is provably optimal by exchange; ties in finish time resolved by smaller original index keep the printed indices minimal. Reconstructing the index list (not just the count) is part of the answer.

examples.explanation: Pick (1,2), (3,4), (5,7), (8,9) — meetings 3 and 6 clash.
Touching endpoints do not conflict under the half-open convention.

constraints: O(N log N) sorting; output is the maximum-size index set

title: Jump Game - I
description:
You are given an integer array nums. You are initially positioned at the array's first index, and each element in the array represents your maximum jump length at that position.

Return true if you can reach the last index, or false otherwise.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
You will always arrive at index 3 no matter what. Its maximum jump length is 0, which makes it impossible to reach the last index.

title: Jump Game II
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array of integers nums of length n. You are initially positioned at index 0.

Each element nums[i] represents the maximum length of a forward jump from index i. In other words, if you are at index i, you can jump to any index (i + j) where:

	• 0 <= j <= nums[i] and

	• i + j < n

Return the minimum number of jumps to reach index n - 1. The test cases are generated such that you can reach index n - 1.

examples.explanation: The minimum number of jumps to reach the last index is 2. Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.

constraints: It's guaranteed that you can reach nums[n - 1].

title: Minimum number of platforms required for a railway
description:
Given arrival and departure times of trains at a station, find the minimum number of platforms so that no train ever waits for a free one.

Sort arrivals and departures independently, then sweep like a merge: an arriving train opens a platform (counter++), a departed train closes one (counter--), tracking the maximum counter reached — that peak is the answer. The boundary rule matters: if a train departs at the same minute another arrives, the arriving one needs a new platform (count arrivals first), or vice versa depending on the statement's turn-around convention. O(N log N).

examples.explanation: Peak overlap of three trains occurs around 0950–1100.
Three trains coexist at 09:00.

constraints: Times as HHMM integers or HH:MM strings; dep > arr per train
State your tie-breaking convention explicitly; O(N log N)

title: Job sequencing Problem
description:
Given N jobs with deadline[i] (a slot 1..deadline must be free) and profit[i], each job takes exactly one unit of time; schedule jobs to maximize total profit, and report how many jobs were done and the profit.

Greedy with a slot table: sort jobs by profit descending; place each job in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline (a disjoint-set "next free slot" pointer makes this near O(N·α)). Skipping a job happens exactly when no such slot is free. The profit-order greedy is optimal for unit-length jobs; DP fails the complexity bar.

examples.explanation: Profit descending: 100 → slot 4, 50 → slot 1, 25 → slot 3, 15 → slot 2; jobs 27 and 19 find no free slot.
Only one slot exists; greedy keeps the maximum profit.

constraints: O(N log N) with sorting + slot search; 64-bit total

title: Candy
description:
There are n children standing in a line.

Each child is assigned a rating value given in the integer array ratings.

You are giving candies to these children subjected to the following requirements:

	• Each child must have at least one candy.

	• Children with a higher rating get more candies than their neighbors.

Return the minimum number of candies you need to have to distribute the candies to the children.

examples.explanation: You can allocate to the first, second and third child with 2, 1, 2 candies respectively.

You can allocate to the first, second and third child with 1, 2, 1 candies respectively.
The third child gets 1 candy because it satisfies the above two conditions.

title: Shortest Job First
description:
Simulate the non-preemptive Shortest Job First scheduler: given burst (execution) times for N processes that all arrive at time 0, order them shortest-first and compute average waiting time and average turnaround time.

Sorting burst times ascending is SJF. Waiting time for a job is the sum of all earlier bursts; turnaround = waiting + its own burst. SJF is provably optimal for minimum average waiting among non-preemptive schedules (exchange argument on any adjacent longer-before-shorter pair). With arrival times involved, a min-heap by burst releases jobs as the clock advances.

examples.explanation: One job never waits.

constraints: O(N log N) sort; print means to two decimals

title: Program for Least Recently Used (LRU) Page Replacement Algorithm
description:
Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache.

Implement the LRUCache class:

	• LRUCache(int capacity) Initialize the LRU cache with positive size capacity.

	• int get(int key) Return the value of the key if the key exists, otherwise return -1.

	• void put(int key, int value) Update the value of the key if the key exists. Otherwise, add the key-value pair to the cache. If the number of keys exceeds the capacity from this operation, evict the least recently used key.

The functions get and put must each run in O(1) average time complexity.
constraints: At most 2 * 105 calls will be made to get and put.

title: Insert Interval
description:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi] represent the start and the end of the ith interval and intervals is sorted in ascending order by starti. Two intervals are considered overlapping if they share at least one point.

Insert newInterval into intervals such that intervals is still sorted in ascending order by starti and intervals still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

Return intervals after the insertion.

Note that you don't need to modify intervals in-place. You can make a new array and return it.

constraints: intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.

Given an array of intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

Note that intervals which only touch at a point are non-overlapping. For example, [1, 2] and [2, 3] are non-overlapping.

title: Pre, Post, Inorder in one traversal
description:
Print the preorder, inorder and postorder traversals of a binary tree in a single traversal visit per node — one DFS that emits each node's value three times, guided by a state marker.

Iterative version: push (root, 1) on a stack; when popping a node with state 1 print it (preorder) and re-push it as state 2 with its right child; on state 2 re-push as state 3 with its left child; state 3 nodes print for the last time (postorder). The three printed sequences are the answer. Recursive variant: one function taking an order parameter. O(n) time, O(n) stack.

examples.explanation: Each node visited three times — before children, between, after.
Leaf emissions coincide.

constraints: One traversal routine must produce all three orders

title: Children Sum Property in Binary Tree
description:
Enforce the children-sum property on a binary tree — every internal node's value must equal the sum of its existing children's values — using only increment operations on node values (each +1 counts as one change). Report the minimum number of changes, or transform the tree in place.

Process bottom-up (postorder): fix both subtrees first. If child-sum exceeds the node, raise the node to the sum; if the node is larger than the child-sum, raise the larger child by the deficit (propagating the increase down that subtree so its own property is restored). One postorder pass is optimal because decrements are forbidden.

Children sum to 5 < 6: add the deficit 1 to the larger child (3 -> 4). Root and children now agree; no root bump is needed.

constraints: Only +1 increments allowed; leaves may be bumped to propagate
Postorder repair; final tree must satisfy the property exactly

title: Requirements needed to construct a unique BT

The constructive view: inorder splits the sequence at each root found from the other traversal — recursion is forced, hence uniqueness. Without inorder there is no way to decide how a preorder's next run of nodes divides between the left and right subtree (the ambiguous case is any node with exactly one child).

title: Check if a tree is a BST or not
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).

A valid BST is defined as follows:

	• The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly less than the node's key.

title: Flood fill algorithm

title: Cycle Detection in Undirected Graph (bfs)

Plain BFS from S: the first time a vertex is dequeued, its BFS depth is the shortest path length, because BFS processes vertices in nondecreasing depth and every edge costs 1. Distances start at -1, dist[S] = 0. O(V + E) — Dijkstra is unnecessary overhead here, and DFS gives no shortest-path guarantee.

title: Shortest path in DAG

Two-step linear algorithm: (1) topologically sort the DAG; (2) relax every edge in topological order — dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w) while sweeping u from sources to sinks. Once a vertex is processed no later edge can improve it. O(V + E), and unlike Dijkstra it also handles negative weights; a cycle would invalidate the sweep, which is exactly why the DAG promise matters.

title: Djisktra's Algorithm

Given a weighted, undirected, connected graph with non-negative edge weights as an adjacency list (V vertices, source 0), compute the shortest distance from the source to every vertex — Dijkstra's algorithm.

Maintain dist[] (∞ except dist[S]=0) and a min-priority queue keyed by distance: extract the closest settled vertex u, relax each edge (u,v,w) with dist[v] > dist[u]+w, pushing improved v. Lazy deletion (skip stale heap entries whose dist already improved) replaces decrease-key. Once popped with the current best distance, a vertex is final — non-negative weights mean no future path can beat it. O((V + E) log V).

examples.explanation: Path 0-2-1 (1+2) beats the direct edge 4; then +1 to 3.

constraints: O((V+E) log V); distances may need 64-bit

title: Why priority Queue is used in Djisktra's Algorithm
description:
Explain (and demonstrate on a trace) why Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue instead of a plain array scan or a FIFO queue: which operation must be fast, what the choice costs per vertex/edge, and what breaks without it.

The greedy step needs the *unvisited vertex with minimum tentative distance* — an array scan finds it in O(V), giving O(V²) total (fine for dense graphs); a min-heap (or std::set/priority_queue) extracts and inserts in O(log V) for O((V+E) log V), dominating on sparse graphs; an ordinary queue loses the ordering guarantee and can settle vertices prematurely. Without decrease-key support, push duplicates and skip stale pops — lazy deletion. The answer should also note the non-negative-weight precondition: Dijkstra itself, heap or not, fails on negative edges.

examples.output: heap version ~O(E log V) ≈ 1.7·10^6 ops vs array O(V²) = 10^10 — heap wins

examples.output: array scan O(V²) matches or beats heap O(E log V)
examples.explanation: log V overhead on V² edges tips it back to the simple implementation.

constraints: Conceptual exercise; include a worked graph trace where a FIFO queue settles a vertex too early
Cover: greedy min-extraction, lazy deletion vs decrease-key, complexity comparison

title: Network Delay Time
description:
You are given a network of n nodes, labeled from 1 to n. You are also given times, a list of travel times as directed edges times[i] = (ui, vi, wi), where ui is the source node, vi is the target node, and wi is the time it takes for a signal to travel from source to target.

We will send a signal from a given node k. Return the minimum time it takes for all the n nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all the n nodes to receive the signal, return -1.
constraints: All the pairs (ui, vi) are unique. (i.e., no multiple edges.)

title: Number of ways to arrive at destination
description:
You are in a city that consists of n intersections numbered from 0 to n - 1 with bi-directional roads between some intersections. The inputs are generated such that you can reach any intersection from any other intersection and that there is at most one road between any two intersections.

You are given an integer n and a 2D integer array roads where roads[i] = [ui, vi, timei] means that there is a road between intersections ui and vi that takes timei minutes to travel. You want to know in how many ways you can travel from intersection 0 to intersection n - 1 in the shortest amount of time.

Return the number of ways you can arrive at your destination in the shortest amount of time. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo 109 + 7.

examples.explanation:
The shortest amount of time it takes to go from intersection 0 to intersection 6 is 7 minutes.
The four ways to get there in 7 minutes are:
- 0 ➝ 6
- 0 ➝ 4 ➝ 6
- 0 ➝ 1 ➝ 2 ➝ 5 ➝ 6
- 0 ➝ 1 ➝ 3 ➝ 5 ➝ 6
There is only one way to go from intersection 0 to intersection 1, and it takes 10 minutes.

constraints: There is at most one road connecting any two intersections.
You can reach any intersection from any other intersection.

title: Minimum multiplications to reach end
description:
Given a start value, a target (end) value, and an array of multipliers, transform start into end by repeatedly replacing the current value x with (x × a[i]) % 100000 for any i. Return the minimum number of multiplications needed, or -1 if end is unreachable. (Striver's 'Minimum Multiplications to reach End'.)

Every value 0..99999 is a node; each of the (≤9) multipliers defines an unweighted directed edge x → (x·a) mod 100000. Shortest path in an unweighted graph = BFS from start over the residue space, dist[] initialized to -1. Building the 10^5×9 edges explicitly is unnecessary — generate neighbours on the fly. O(100000 × k).

examples.explanation: 2×2 = 4 then 4×7 = 28 (or 2×7 = 14, 14×2 = 28); one multiplication is not enough ({4, 10, 14} excludes 28).
Every reachable residue is 9·2^k mod 100000 — the factor 9 can never vanish, so 2 is unreachable.

constraints: O(100000 × k) BFS over the residue graph

title: Bellman Ford Algorithm
description:
Given a weighted directed graph with V vertices, M edges (u, v, w) where w may be negative, and source 0, find the shortest distances to all vertices; return {-1} if the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable in a way that improves paths. (GFG Bellman-Ford formulation.)

Relax all M edges V-1 times: after i passes, every shortest path with ≤ i edges is finalized — a simple path uses at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds suffice whether or not negative edges exist. One extra pass: any edge that still relaxes proves a negative cycle. O(V·M) — slower than Dijkstra but strictly more expressive (negative edges), and it detects the cases where shortest paths are undefined.

examples.explanation: dist[2] = min(4, 5-2) = 3 by pass 2; dist[4] = 6; dist[3] = min(3+6, 6+2) = 8. Negative edge 1→2 handled fine.
Cycle 1→2→1 costs -5: pass V still relaxes edge 2→1, proving a negative cycle.

constraints: O(V·M); report [-1] on any negative cycle found in pass V

title: Floyd warshall algorithm
description:
Given a weighted directed graph as an adjacency matrix (adj[i][j] = weight, or -1 for 'no edge', zero diagonal), compute the shortest distance between every ordered pair of vertices — the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs DP.

dist[i][j] = min over all intermediate sets { paths using vertices 0..k as intermediates }, updated k-in-the-outer-loop: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). The k-major loop order is mandatory (it is the DP stage, not an interchangeable nesting). Initialize with edge weights and 0 diagonal; translate unreachable pairs to -1 on output (per GFG convention). O(V³) time, O(V²) space; detects negative cycles when dist[i][i] < 0 appears.

examples.explanation: Via vertex 1: 0→1→2 costs 1+7 = 8, beating the direct 43; vertex 2 has no outgoing edges so its row keeps -1s.
1→0→2 gives dist[1][2] = 2+3 = 5; the 2↔0 and 2→1 pairs stay unreachable.

constraints: O(V³) triple loop, k outermost; print 0 on diagonal

title: Find the city with the smallest number of neighbors
description:
There are n cities numbered from 0 to n-1. Given the array edges where edges[i] = [fromi, toi, weighti] represents a bidirectional and weighted edge between cities fromi and toi, and given the integer distanceThreshold.

Return the city with the smallest number of cities that are reachable through some path and whose distance is at most distanceThreshold, If there are multiple such cities, return the city with the greatest number.

Notice that the distance of a path connecting cities i and j is equal to the sum of the edges' weights along that path.

examples.explanation:
The figure above describes the graph. 
The neighboring cities at a distanceThreshold = 4 for each city are:
City 0 -> [City 1, City 2] 
City 1 -> [City 0, City 2, City 3] 
City 2 -> [City 0, City 1, City 3] 
City 3 -> [City 1, City 2] 
Cities 0 and 3 have 2 neighboring cities at a distanceThreshold = 4, but we have to return city 3 since it has the greatest number.

The figure above describes the graph. 
The neighboring cities at a distanceThreshold = 2 for each city are:
City 0 -> [City 1] 
City 1 -> [City 0, City 4] 
City 2 -> [City 3, City 4] 
City 3 -> [City 2, City 4]
City 4 -> [City 1, City 2, City 3] 
The city 0 has 1 neighboring city at a distanceThreshold = 2.

title: Prim's Algorithm
description:
Given a weighted, connected, undirected graph as an adjacency list (V vertices, E edges), compute the total weight of its Minimum Spanning Tree using Prim's algorithm.

Grow one tree from vertex 0: keep a min-heap of candidate edges crossing the cut; repeatedly pop the cheapest edge, and if it leads to an unvisited vertex, add its weight, mark that vertex, and push all its outgoing edges. Each vertex joins once → V-1 accepted edges. O((V + E) log V) with the heap (dense-graph O(V²) array variant scans min key). Correct by the cut property: the lightest edge across any cut is safe for the MST.

examples.explanation: Single forced edge.

constraints: O((V+E) log V); skip stale heap entries for visited vertices

title: Disjoint Set
description:
Implement a Disjoint Set Union (union-find) structure over n elements 0..n-1 supporting find(x) (which component?), union(x, y) (merge components) and component count/size queries — with path compression and union by rank (or size) so operations run in effectively constant amortized time.

Each component is a rooted tree: find walks parent[] up to the root; path compression re-points every visited node directly at the root. Union attaches the smaller-rank (or smaller-size) root under the larger — keeping trees shallow. α(n) inverse-Ackermann amortized bound. Application follow-ups: Kruskal MST, cycle detection in undirected graphs (union finds two endpoints already together), account-merge style grouping problems.

examples.input: union(0,1), union(2,3), union(1,2), find(3) then find(0)
examples.explanation: Second union merges the two pairs; ranks keep the tree depth ≤ 2.

examples.input: union(4,5), then query find(4) == find(5)? find(4) == find(0)?
examples.explanation: Two separate components remain.

constraints: Both find and union amortized O(α(n)); parent + rank/size arrays only

title: Find the MST weight
description:
Given a connected, weighted, undirected graph with V vertices and E edges (u, v, weight), return the total weight of its Minimum Spanning Tree — the acyclic edge subset connecting all vertices of minimum summed weight. Solve with Kruskal: sort edges by weight, then greedily accept an edge whenever its endpoints lie in different components (DSU), stopping at V-1 accepted edges.

Sorting dominates at O(E log E); each union/find is near O(1) via path compression + rank. Correct via the cut/cycle property: skipping an edge whose endpoints are already connected can never force a more expensive future choice. The Prim variant (heap over frontier edges, O((V+E) log V)) is the sibling solution.

examples.explanation: Cheapest two edges; the third closes a cycle.

constraints: O(E log E) with DSU; result fits in 64-bit

title: Number of operations to make network connected
description:
There are n computers numbered from 0 to n - 1 connected by ethernet cables connections forming a network where connections[i] = [ai, bi] represents a connection between computers ai and bi. Any computer can reach any other computer directly or indirectly through the network.

You are given an initial computer network connections. You can extract certain cables between two directly connected computers, and place them between any pair of disconnected computers to make them directly connected.

Return the minimum number of times you need to do this in order to make all the computers connected. If it is not possible, return -1.

examples.explanation: Remove cable between computer 1 and 2 and place between computers 1 and 3.
There are not enough cables.

constraints: No two computers are connected by more than one cable.

title: Most stones removed with same row or column
description:
On a 2D plane, we place n stones at some integer coordinate points. Each coordinate point may have at most one stone.

A stone can be removed if it shares either the same row or the same column as another stone that has not been removed.

Given an array stones of length n where stones[i] = [xi, yi] represents the location of the ith stone, return the largest possible number of stones that can be removed.

examples.explanation:
One way to remove 5 stones is as follows:
1. Remove stone [2,2] because it shares the same row as [2,1].
2. Remove stone [2,1] because it shares the same column as [0,1].
3. Remove stone [1,2] because it shares the same row as [1,0].
4. Remove stone [1,0] because it shares the same column as [0,0].
5. Remove stone [0,1] because it shares the same row as [0,0].
Stone [0,0] cannot be removed since it does not share a row/column with another stone still on the plane.

One way to make 3 moves is as follows:
1. Remove stone [2,2] because it shares the same row as [2,0].
2. Remove stone [2,0] because it shares the same column as [0,0].
3. Remove stone [0,2] because it shares the same row as [0,0].
Stones [0,0] and [1,1] cannot be removed since they do not share a row/column with another stone still on the plane.
[0,0] is the only stone on the plane, so you cannot remove it.

constraints: No two stones are at the same coordinate point.

title: Accounts merge
description:
Given a list of accounts where each element accounts[i] is a list of strings, where the first element accounts[i][0] is a name, and the rest of the elements are emails representing emails of the account.

Now, we would like to merge these accounts. Two accounts definitely belong to the same person if there is some common email to both accounts. Note that even if two accounts have the same name, they may belong to different people as people could have the same name. A person can have any number of accounts initially, but all of their accounts definitely have the same name.

After merging the accounts, return the accounts in the following format: the first element of each account is the name, and the rest of the elements are emails in sorted order. The accounts themselves can be returned in any order.

examples.explanation:
The first and second John's are the same person as they have the common email "johnsmith@mail.com".
The third John and Mary are different people as none of their email addresses are used by other accounts.
We could return these lists in any order, for example the answer [['Mary', 'mary@mail.com'], ['John', 'johnnybravo@mail.com'], 
['John', 'john00@mail.com', 'john_newyork@mail.com', 'johnsmith@mail.com']] would still be accepted.

constraints: accounts[i][j] (for j > 0) is a valid email.

title: Number of islands II
description:
Start with an empty m × n grid of water; each query adds land at one cell. After every addition, report the number of islands (4-connected groups of land cells). Queries are online — islands may merge when a bridge cell arrives.

Disjoint-set union over land cells: a new cell starts as its own component (count += 1), then union with each of its four land neighbors, decrementing the count on every successful merge. Path compression + union by rank makes it O(q α(mn)). Re-BFS per query is the slow baseline.

examples.explanation: (1,1) is adjacent to both (0,0) and (0,2): it joins a new component (+1) then merges two (−2), dropping the count from 3 to 1. (2,0) and (2,2) each start a fresh island (not 4-adjacent to anything).
Diagonal cells are not 4-adjacent — no merge.

constraints: O(m·n + q α) expected; report after each query, not just the end

title: Making a large island
description:
You are given an n x n binary matrix grid. You are allowed to change at most one 0 to be 1.

Return the size of the largest island in grid after applying this operation.

An island is a 4-directionally connected group of 1s.

title: Swim in Rising Water
description:
You are given an n x n integer matrix grid where each value grid[i][j] represents the elevation at that point (i, j).

It starts raining, and water gradually rises over time. At time t, the water level is t, meaning any cell with elevation less than equal to t is submerged or reachable.

You can swim from a square to another 4-directionally adjacent square if and only if the elevation of both squares individually are at most t. You can swim infinite distances in zero time. Of course, you must stay within the boundaries of the grid during your swim.

Return the minimum time until you can reach the bottom right square (n - 1, n - 1) if you start at the top left square (0, 0).

3
Explanation:

You cannot go anywhere else because 4-directionally adjacent neighbors have a higher elevation than t = 0.
You cannot reach point (1, 1) until time 3.

title: Bridges in graph
description:
There are n servers numbered from 0 to n - 1 connected by undirected server-to-server connections forming a network where connections[i] = [ai, bi] represents a connection between servers ai and bi. Any server can reach other servers directly or indirectly through the network.

A critical connection is a connection that, if removed, will make some servers unable to reach some other server.

Return all critical connections in the network in any order.

title: Articulation point in graph
description:
Find all articulation points (cut vertices) of a connected undirected graph — vertices whose removal increases the number of connected components. (GFG articulation-point formulation; print them sorted.)

One DFS computing disc[u] (discovery time) and low[u] (earliest discovery reachable from u's subtree using ≤ one back edge). u is an articulation point if: (a) u is the DFS root with ≥ 2 DFS children, or (b) u is non-root and has a child v with low[v] >= disc[u] — v's subtree cannot reach above u. Mark each u once despite multiple triggering children. O(V + E). Bridges use the stricter test low[v] > disc[u].

examples.explanation: Removing 1 or 3 disconnects the graph; the triangle 0-1-2 shields its other vertices (low values fall below discovery times).
Every vertex stays connected after one removal; no articulation points.

constraints: 0 <= E <= 10^5; undirected connected (run DFS per component if not)
O(V + E) single DFS; skip only the direct parent edge once

title: Kosaraju's algorithm
description:
Given a string s of lowercase letters, you need to find the maximum number of non-empty substrings of s that meet the following conditions:

	• The substrings do not overlap, that is for any two substrings s[i..j] and s[x..y], either j < x or i > y is true.

	• A substring that contains a certain character c must also contain all occurrences of c.

Find the maximum number of substrings that meet the above conditions. If there are multiple solutions with the same number of substrings, return the one with minimum total length. It can be shown that there exists a unique solution of minimum total length.

Notice that you can return the substrings in any order.

examples.output:
["e","f","ccc"]
Explanation: The following are all the possible substrings that meet the conditions:
[
  "adefaddaccc"
  "adefadda",
  "ef",
  "e",
  "f",
  "ccc",
]
If we choose the first string, we cannot choose anything else and we'd get only 1. If we choose "adefadda", we are left with "ccc" which is the only one that doesn't overlap, thus obtaining 2 substrings. Notice also, that it's not optimal to choose "ef" since it can be split into two. Therefore, the optimal way is to choose ["e","f","ccc"] which gives us 3 substrings. No other solution of the same number of substrings exist.

["d","bb","cc"]
Explanation: Notice that while the set of substrings ["d","abba","cc"] also has length 3, it's considered incorrect since it has larger total length.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.

title: Climbing stairs
description:
You are climbing a staircase. It takes n steps to reach the top.

Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

examples.explanation:
There are two ways to climb to the top.
1. 1 step + 1 step
2. 2 steps

There are three ways to climb to the top.
1. 1 step + 1 step + 1 step
2. 1 step + 2 steps
3. 2 steps + 1 step

title: Frog Jump
description:
A frog stands on stone 0 of n stones with heights h[0..n-1]; it may jump 1 or 2 stones forward, paying |h[i] - h[j]| energy per jump. Find the minimum total energy to reach stone n-1. (Classic 1D DP introduction.)

dp[i] = minimum energy to stand on stone i: dp[0] = 0, dp[1] = |h1-h0|, and dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + |h[i]-h[i-1]|, dp[i-2] + |h[i]-h[i-2]|). O(n) time; reduce to two rolling variables for O(1) space. Recursion + memo is the teaching path, tabulation the expected answer.

examples.explanation: Only route: 10→20→30 costs 10 + 10.

constraints: O(n) time; O(1) space with rolling variables

title: Frog jump with K distances
description:
Extend the frog jump: the frog can now jump any distance from 1 to k stones ahead, still paying |h[i] - h[j]| per jump. Minimum energy to reach the last of n stones.

dp[i] = min over j = 1..min(k, i) of dp[i-j] + |h[i] - h[i-j]|. O(n·k) time — the k = 2 case is the previous exercise. Space O(n) for the table, or a sliding window of k values for O(k). Reading input: T test cases with n, k, then heights.

A monotone-queue trick (two deques tracking dp[j] ± h[j]) can reach O(n), but the sheet expects the direct O(n·k) recurrence.

Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

Rob house 1 (money = 2), rob house 3 (money = 9) and rob house 5 (money = 1).
Total amount you can rob = 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.

title: House robber
description:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. All houses at this place are arranged in a circle. That means the first house is the neighbor of the last one. Meanwhile, adjacent houses have a security system connected, and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

examples.explanation: You cannot rob house 1 (money = 2) and then rob house 3 (money = 2), because they are adjacent houses.

Rob house 1 (money = 1) and then rob house 3 (money = 3).

title: Ninja's training
description:
Ninja has N days and three tasks (A, B, C); points[d][t] is the points earned doing task t on day d. Each day he does exactly one task, and the same task cannot be done on two consecutive days. Maximize total points over the N days.

State = (day, last task done): dp[d][t] = points[d][t] + max over t' ≠ t of dp[d-1][t']. Base: day 0 is just points[0][t]. Answer = max over t of dp[N-1][t]. O(N·3·2) time; the 'can't repeat yesterday' constraint lives entirely in the last-task state — the lesson of the problem. Space reduces to the previous row (or 4 variables).

examples.explanation: Single day, no adjacency constraint.

title: Grid Unique Paths : DP on Grids (DP8)

There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.

Given the two integers m and n, return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner.

The test cases are generated so that the answer will be less than or equal to 2 * 109.

examples.explanation:
From the top-left corner, there are a total of 3 ways to reach the bottom-right corner:
1. Right -> Down -> Down
2. Down -> Down -> Right
3. Down -> Right -> Down

title: Unique paths II
description:
You are given an m x n integer array grid. There is a robot initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.

An obstacle and space are marked as 1 or 0 respectively in grid. A path that the robot takes cannot include any square that is an obstacle.

Return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner.

The testcases are generated so that the answer will be less than or equal to 2 * 109.

examples.explanation:
There is one obstacle in the middle of the 3x3 grid above.
There are two ways to reach the bottom-right corner:
1. Right -> Right -> Down -> Down
2. Down -> Down -> Right -> Right

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
description:
Given a m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top left to bottom right, which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path.

Note: You can only move either down or right at any point in time.

title: Triangle

Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom.

For each step, you may move to an adjacent number of the row below. More formally, if you are on index i on the current row, you may move to either index i or index i + 1 on the next row.

title: Ninja and his Friends
description:
A grid of N rows × M columns holds cherries (0..1000 per cell). Three ninjas start at the top row — columns 0, M/2 (middle) and M-1 — and descend to the bottom row; from (r, c) each may move to (r+1, c-1), (r+1, c) or (r+1, c+1). When two or three land on the same cell, its cherries are collected once. Maximize total cherries collected.

DP over rows with the column triple as state: dp[c1][c2][c3] = best total up to the current row with the ninjas at those columns. Transition enumerates all 3³ = 27 next-column combinations, adding the cherries of the distinct target cells (the 'collect once' rule handled by deduplicating the up-to-3 columns). O(N·M³·27); memory two rows. Without the sharing rule the problem would split into three independent path DPs — the coupling is the point.

examples.explanation: Row 0 collects 2+3+1 = 6; best spread on row 1 is columns 0,1,2 again (all can reach their own column): 1+5+1 = 7; total 13.
One row: start positions are the answer, all distinct.

constraints: 1 <= N <= 100, 3 <= M <= 20 (M odd so a middle column exists)
O(N·M³) time, O(M³) or two-row space

title: Subset sum equal to target (DP- 14)
description:
Given an array of positive integers and a target sum, decide whether some subset sums exactly to the target. Return true/false (0/1).

Subset-sum is the 0/1 knapsack decision form: dp[i][s] = using first i items, can sum s be made? Transitions: skip (dp[i-1][s]) or take (dp[i-1][s - arr[i-1]], valid when s ≥ arr[i-1]). Base dp[·][0] = true, dp[0][>0] = false. O(n·target) time, O(target) with a bitset or a descending-s 1D array. (The sheet labels it DP-14; meet-in-the-middle is the alternative for large targets, small n.)

examples.explanation: Total sum 6 < 7.

title: Partition equal subset sum
description: Given an integer array nums, return true if you can partition the array into two subsets such that the sum of the elements in both subsets is equal or false otherwise.

examples.explanation: The array can be partitioned as [1, 5, 5] and [11].
The array cannot be partitioned into equal sum subsets.

title: Partition a set into two subsets with minimum absolute sum difference
description:
You are given an integer array nums of 2 * n integers. You need to partition nums into two arrays of length n to minimize the absolute difference of the sums of the arrays. To partition nums, put each element of nums into one of the two arrays.

Return the minimum possible absolute difference.

examples.explanation:
One optimal partition is: [3,9] and [7,3].
The absolute difference between the sums of the arrays is abs((3 + 9) - (7 + 3)) = 2.

One optimal partition is: [-36] and [36].
The absolute difference between the sums of the arrays is abs((-36) - (36)) = 72.

One optimal partition is: [2,4,-9] and [-1,0,-2].
The absolute difference between the sums of the arrays is abs((2 + 4 + -9) - (-1 + 0 + -2)) = 0.

title: Count subsets with sum K
description:
Count the subsets of an array of positive integers whose sum equals a given goal; return the count modulo 10^9 + 7 (Striver DP-16 form: every index-distinct selection counts, including the empty subset when goal = 0).

Same 0/1 table as subset-sum but counting: dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s] + dp[i-1][s - arr[i]] (ways skipping + ways taking). O(n·goal) time, O(goal) space rolling row. Zeros in the input double the counts per zero — the DP handles them naturally.

examples.explanation: {first 2, 3}, {second 2, 3} and {1, 2, 2} — the two 2s are distinct elements, counted by index.
C(4,2) equal-sum pairs.

title: Count partitions with given difference
description:
Partition an array of non-negative integers into two subsets S1 and S2 so that S1 - S2 = given difference (S1 ≥ S2); count the number of ways, modulo 10^9 + 7.

Let total = Σarr. S1 + S2 = total and S1 - S2 = d ⇒ S2 = (total - d)/2 — so the problem *reduces* to counting subsets with sum (total-d)/2, the previous exercise, when (total - d) is even and non-negative; otherwise 0. The all-zero subtlety: zeros can join either side, so each zero doubles the count (or let the DP handle them naturally: a zero adds dp[s] to itself → ×2 per zero). O(n·total/2).

title: Assign Cookies
description:

If s[j] >= g[i], we can assign the cookie j to the child i, and the child i will be content. Your goal is to maximize the number of your content children and output the maximum number.

You need to output 1.

You have 2 children and 3 cookies. The greed factors of 2 children are 1, 2.

title: Unbounded knapsack
description:
Unbounded knapsack: given n item types (value, weight) and capacity W, maximize total value using any number of copies of each type without exceeding weight. Return the maximum value.

dp[w] = max over items i with weight_i ≤ w of dp[w - weight_i] + value_i — the *same row* feeds itself (that is what 'unbounded' means: take item i, stay able to take it again), so the w-loop ascends and the item-loop may be either order (dp over capacities with inner item scan). O(n·W). Contrast with 0/1 knapsack where ascending w is forbidden. A dominated item (≥ weight, ≤ value) can be pruned first.

title: Rod Cutting Problem | (DP - 24)
description:
Rod Cutting (DP-24): a rod of length n must be cut into integer-length pieces; price[i] is the selling price of a piece of length i (i = 1..n, given 1-indexed or as a value array for lengths 1..n). Maximize the total revenue. (Equivalently: unbounded knapsack with weight = value-index = length.)

Revenue(len) = max over first cut k = 1..len of price[k] + Revenue(len - k), with Revenue(0) = 0 — O(n²) tabulation. The identity cut (sell the whole rod) is always a candidate, so an optimal solution may cut zero pieces. The sheet also frames the equivalent form where piece i has length cut[i] and value price[i] — then it is literally unbounded knapsack over capacities 1..n.

description:

description:

title: Longest common substring

title: Best time to buy and sell stock
description:
You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0.

examples.explanation:

title: Best time to buy and sell stock II
description:
You are given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day.

On each day, you may decide to buy and/or sell the stock. You can only hold at most one share of the stock at any time. However, you can sell and buy the stock multiple times on the same day, ensuring you never hold more than one share of the stock.

Find and return the maximum profit you can achieve.

examples.explanation:
Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 3 (price = 5), profit = 5-1 = 4.
Then buy on day 4 (price = 3) and sell on day 5 (price = 6), profit = 6-3 = 3.
Total profit is 4 + 3 = 7.

Buy on day 1 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 5), profit = 5-1 = 4.
Total profit is 4.

title: Best time to buy and sell stock III

Both must actually emit the sequence.

examples.explanation: Parent-pointer reconstruction from the DP.
Strictly decreasing arrays have no increasing pair.

Print one valid LIS; length must be maximal

wordA is a predecessor of wordB if and only if we can insert exactly one letter anywhere in wordA without changing the order of the other characters to make it equal to wordB.

	• For example, "abc" is a predecessor of "abac", while "cba" is not a predecessor of "bcad".

A word chain is a sequence of words [word1, word2, ..., wordk] with k >= 1, where word1 is a predecessor of word2, word2 is a predecessor of word3, and so on. A single word is trivially a word chain with k == 1.

Return the length of the longest possible word chain with words chosen from the given list of words.

Compute forward LIS lengths lis[i] (longest increasing run ending at i) and backward lengths lds[i] (longest decreasing run starting at i, i.e. LIS scanning right-to-left), via the O(n²) DP or O(n log n). Every index is a candidate peak: answer = max over i of lis[i] + lds[i] - 1. Bitonic *subsequence*, not substring.

title: Matrix chain multiplication
description:
Given the dimension array arr[0..n-1] — n matrices M_i of size arr[i] × arr[i+1] — find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the parenthesization. (Matrix Chain Multiplication, top-down.)

Cost of multiplying p×q by q×r is p·q·r. dp(i, j) = min over split k of dp(i,k) + dp(k+1,j) + arr[i-1]·arr[k]·arr[j] for the range M_i..M_j (1-indexed matrices), base dp(i,i) = 0. Memoized recursion O(n³); the order of multiplication matters enormously — 10×30, 30×5, 5×60: (AB)C costs 1500+3000 = 4500 vs A(BC) 18000+1500 = 19500, a 4.3× gap.

examples.explanation: Single multiplication 10·20·30.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication | Bottom-Up|(DP-49)

Matrix Chain Multiplication, bottom-up (DP-49): same cost problem as the top-down version — minimum scalar multiplications to parenthesize n matrices with dimensions arr — implemented as tabulation instead of recursion, and typically also asked alongside printing the optimal parenthesization via a split table.

Fill by chain length: for len = 2..n, for i descending (or ascending) with j = i+len-1, dp[i][j] = min over k in [i, j) of dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]·arr[k]·arr[j]). The length-major loop guarantees every sub-range is solved before its parent. Store argmin k in a split matrix and emit parentheses with a recursive print(split, i, j). Bottom-up removes stack depth and matches the memo version's O(n³).

examples.explanation: One multiplication.

constraints: O(n³) tabulation; length outer, start inner; split table for reconstruction

If you burst the ith balloon, you will get nums[i - 1] * nums[i] * nums[i + 1] coins. If i - 1 or i + 1 goes out of bounds of the array, then treat it as if there is a balloon with a 1 painted on it.

title: Different Ways to Evaluate a Boolean Expression
description:
A boolean expression is an expression that evaluates to either true or false. It can be in one of the following shapes:

	• 't' that evaluates to true.

	• 'f' that evaluates to false.

	• '!(subExpr)' that evaluates to the logical NOT of the inner expression subExpr.

	• '&(subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn)' that evaluates to the logical AND of the inner expressions subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn where n >= 1.

	• '|(subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn)' that evaluates to the logical OR of the inner expressions subExpr1, subExpr2, ..., subExprn where n >= 1.

Given a string expression that represents a boolean expression, return the evaluation of that expression.

It is guaranteed that the given expression is valid and follows the given rules.

First, evaluate &(f,t) --> (false AND true) --> false --> f. The expression is now "!(f)".
Then, evaluate !(f) --> NOT false --> true. We return true.

title: Trie Implementation and Operations
description:
A trie (pronounced as "try") or prefix tree is a tree data structure used to efficiently store and retrieve keys in a dataset of strings. There are various applications of this data structure, such as autocomplete and spellchecker.

Implement the Trie class:

	• Trie() Initializes the trie object.

	• void insert(String word) Inserts the string word into the trie.

	• boolean search(String word) Returns true if the string word is in the trie (i.e., was inserted before), and false otherwise.

title: Trie Implementation and Advanced Operations
description:
Implement a Trie (prefix tree) over lowercase English letters supporting: insert(word), search(word) → does the exact word exist?, startsWith(prefix) → is it a prefix of any stored word?, and the advanced operations — delete(word) and countWords(prefix).

Each node stores up to 26 child pointers and an endOfWord flag; insert walks/slots down one char per level; search must additionally check the terminal flag (a present path alone only proves prefixhood). Delete = walk down recording the last node with >1 child (or a terminal), then prune the unshared suffix. count(prefix) walks to the prefix node and sums terminals in its subtree — precompute a subtree word-count field per node to answer in O(|prefix|). Time is proportional to word length for every operation; space O(total inserted characters).

title: Number of distinct substrings in a string
description:
Count the number of distinct substrings of a string (two substrings count once even if they occur at different positions).

Trie route: for each suffix, insert into a trie and count how many nodes had to be newly created — the running total is the answer, O(n²) nodes/time. Suffix-array route: total substrings n(n+1)/2 minus the sum of LCP values between consecutive sorted suffixes, O(n log n) or O(n). Both are expected answers; the suffix array one scales past 10^4.

examples.explanation: Distinct classes: a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab, baba, ababa.
a, aa, aaa — repeats collapse.

constraints: Exclude the empty substring from the count

title: Bit PreRequisites for TRIE Problems
description:
Bit prerequisites for binary-Trie problems: work fluently with the fixed-width binary view of integers that maximum-XOR / minimum-XOR trie queries rest on — extract bit i of x as (x >> i) & 1, read numbers MSB-first (bit 31 down to 0 for 32-bit ints), and use XOR identities: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and a set bit in the xor result means the operands differ at that position.

The exercises: print the 32-bit representation of given integers, compute pairwise XORs, and reason why a greedy MSB-first walk maximizes a XOR against a stored set (at each level prefer the opposite bit — it sets a higher-order 1 which dominates all lower bits combined). This warm-up makes the binary trie (max-XOR query) mechanical: bits are just the alphabet {0,1}.

examples.explanation: (5 >> i) & 1 for each i isolates bit i; for 32-bit ints run i = 31 down to 0.
5^1 = 4, 5^4 = 1, 5^7 = 2. Greedily the top differing bit wins: 5 = 101, preferring y with bit-2 = 0 (y = 1) sets the 4's place, which outweighs everything below.

constraints: Bit indices 30 down to 0 are enough for non-negative ints
No trie required yet — pure bit manipulation drills

title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array
description: Given an integer array nums, return the maximum result of nums[i] XOR nums[j], where 0 <= i <= j < n.

examples.explanation: The maximum result is 5 XOR 25 = 28.

title: Maximum Xor with an element from an array
description:
You are given an array nums consisting of non-negative integers. You are also given a queries array, where queries[i] = [xi, mi].

The answer to the ith query is the maximum bitwise XOR value of xi and any element of nums that does not exceed mi. In other words, the answer is max(nums[j] XOR xi) for all j such that nums[j] <= mi. If all elements in nums are larger than mi, then the answer is -1.

Return an integer array answer where answer.length == queries.length and answer[i] is the answer to the ith query.

examples.explanation:
1) 0 and 1 are the only two integers not greater than 1. 0 XOR 3 = 3 and 1 XOR 3 = 2. The larger of the two is 3.
2) 1 XOR 2 = 3.
3) 5 XOR 2 = 7.

title: Minimum number of bracket reversals to make an expression balanced
description:
A parentheses string is valid if and only if:

	• It is the empty string,

	• It can be written as AB (A concatenated with B), where A and B are valid strings, or

	• It can be written as (A), where A is a valid string.

You are given a parentheses string s. In one move, you can insert a parenthesis at any position of the string.

	• For example, if s = "()))", you can insert an opening parenthesis to be "(()))" or a closing parenthesis to be "())))".

Return the minimum number of moves required to make s valid.

title: Count and say
description:
The count-and-say sequence is a sequence of digit strings defined by the recursive formula:

	• countAndSay(1) = "1"

	• countAndSay(n) is the run-length encoding of countAndSay(n - 1).

Run-length encoding (RLE) is a string compression method that works by replacing each maximal group of consecutive identical characters with the concatenation of the length of the group followed by the character itself. For example, to compress the string "3322251" we replace "33" with "23", replace "222" with "32", replace "5" with "15", and replace "1" with "11". Thus the compressed string becomes "23321511".

Given a positive integer n, return the nth element of the count-and-say sequence.

examples.explanation:
countAndSay(1) = "1"
countAndSay(2) = RLE of "1" = "11"
countAndSay(3) = RLE of "11" = "21"
countAndSay(4) = RLE of "21" = "1211"

title: Rabin Karp Algorithm
description:
Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of times you should repeat string a so that string b is a substring of it. If it is impossible for b​​​​​​ to be a substring of a after repeating it, return -1.

Notice: string "abc" repeated 0 times is "", repeated 1 time is "abc" and repeated 2 times is "abcabc".

examples.explanation: We return 3 because by repeating a three times "abcdabcdabcd", b is a substring of it.

constraints: a and b consist of lowercase English letters.

title: Z function
description: Compute the Z-array of a string s of length n: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of s (Z[0] is conventionally 0 or n). Use it for linear pattern search: build Z on pattern + '#' + text — any position with Z-value |pattern| is an occurrence.

examples.explanation: i=1: "aabaab" shares "aa" with the prefix, breaks at b vs a; i=4: "aab" shares "aa"; single letters elsewhere.
i=2: "abcab" matches prefix "ab" then c ≠ a; i=5: "ab" matches to the end of string.

constraints: Lowercase alphabet; separator '#' must not appear in pattern/text

title: KMP Algorithm or LPS array
description:
Implement KMP: precompute the LPS (longest proper prefix which is also suffix) array for a pattern, then search a text in linear time, never backtracking the text pointer.

LPS construction: lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pat[0..i] equal to its suffix, built by falling back j = lps[j-1] on mismatches. Search mirrors it: on mismatch between text[i] and pattern[j], retry with j = lps[j-1] (a matched border stays matched); emit a hit whenever j reaches |pattern| and continue with j = lps[j-1] to allow overlaps. O(n + m); the naive O(n·m) scan is what the automaton view eliminates.

examples.explanation: LPS = [0,0,1,2,0,1,2,3,4]; after matching ABAB at text[10..13] a mismatch-free run completes the pattern at 18 — fallbacks at earlier D/C mismatches reuse the ABAB border instead of rewinding the text pointer.
Overlapping hits: after a match j resets to lps[1] = 1.

constraints: O(n + m) time, O(m) extra for LPS

title: Shortest Palindrome
description:
You are given a string s. You can convert s to a palindrome by adding characters in front of it.

Return the shortest palindrome you can find by performing this transformation.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.

title: Longest happy prefix
description:
A string is called a happy prefix if it is a non-empty prefix which is also a suffix (excluding itself).

Given a string s, return the longest happy prefix of s. Return an empty string "" if no such prefix exists.

examples.explanation: s contains 4 prefix excluding itself ("l", "le", "lev", "leve"), and suffix ("l", "el", "vel", "evel"). The largest prefix which is also suffix is given by "l".
"abab" is the largest prefix which is also suffix. They can overlap in the original string.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.

title: Count Palindromic Subsequences
description:
Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it.

A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward.

A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.

examples.explanation: Three palindromic strings: "a", "b", "c".
Six palindromic strings: "a", "a", "a", "aa", "aa", "aaa".

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
